facts.title: Found on the Sun first
facts.text: Helium is the only element discovered in space before it was found on Earth. During a total solar eclipse on 18 August 1868, astronomers Jules Janssen and Norman Lockyer detected a bright yellow spectral line in the Sun's atmosphere that matched no known element. Lockyer named it after the Greek word 'helios', meaning Sun.

facts.title: The reluctant noble gas
facts.text: Helium has a completely filled outer electron shell with just two electrons, making it the most chemically inert element known. It forms no stable compounds under normal conditions and does not react with any other substance. This is why it is grouped with the noble gases despite having only two electrons rather than eight in its outer shell.

facts.title: Never freezes on its own
facts.text: Helium is the only element that cannot be frozen solid at normal atmospheric pressure, no matter how cold it gets. Even at absolute zero, it remains a liquid because its atoms have such weak attractions and large quantum motion. To make solid helium you must apply about 25 atmospheres of pressure while keeping it below roughly 1 kelvin.

facts.title: A liquid that climbs walls
facts.text: When cooled below 2.17 kelvin, liquid helium-4 becomes a 'superfluid' with zero viscosity. In this state it can flow through microscopic cracks, creep up and over the walls of its container as a thin film, and even form a frictionless fountain. This bizarre behavior is a rare large-scale display of quantum mechanics, and its discovery led to a Nobel Prize for Pyotr Kapitsa.

facts.title: Born inside the Big Bang
facts.text: About a quarter of all ordinary matter in the universe by mass is helium, making it the second most abundant element after hydrogen. Most of it was created in the first few minutes after the Big Bang, before any stars existed. Stars like our Sun also produce helium continuously by fusing hydrogen in their cores.

facts.title: Why your voice goes squeaky
facts.text: Breathing helium temporarily raises the pitch of your voice because sound travels nearly three times faster through helium than through ordinary air. The faster speed changes which frequencies your vocal tract amplifies, producing that famous cartoon-like sound. It is not entirely harmless, though, since inhaling pure helium displaces oxygen and can cause suffocation.

facts.title: It cools the MRI machines
facts.text: The powerful superconducting magnets inside hospital MRI scanners are kept working by liquid helium at around 4 kelvin, close to absolute zero. Helium is the only practical coolant cold enough for this job, and a single scanner can hold over a thousand litres of it. This makes medical imaging one of the largest industrial uses of the element.

facts.title: It escapes into space forever
facts.text: Helium is so light that once released into the atmosphere it drifts to the top and gradually leaks into outer space, never to return. Because of this, Earth's helium is a genuinely finite resource that comes mainly from the slow radioactive decay of uranium and thorium deep underground. It is extracted from natural gas wells, with the United States, Qatar, and Algeria among the leading producers.

facts.title: Alpha particles are helium
facts.text: An alpha particle emitted during radioactive decay is simply a helium nucleus, made of two protons and two neutrons with no electrons. As these particles slow down and capture electrons, they become ordinary helium atoms. This is the main natural source of the helium trapped in Earth's crust over billions of years.

facts.title: Deep divers breathe it
facts.text: Professional and deep-sea divers often breathe special mixtures such as heliox, which replaces some or most of the nitrogen in their air with helium. Helium does not cause the dangerous 'nitrogen narcosis' that impairs judgement at depth, and it makes the breathing gas less dense and easier to inhale under high pressure. Similar oxygen-helium blends are also used medically to help patients with severe airway obstructions breathe more easily.
